01 — Why mark with a laser

A label can fall off. A laser mark cannot.

Traceability fails at the weakest physical link. A printed label is an adhesive film sitting on top of the solder mask; an inkjet code is chemistry deposited on the surface. Both are additions, and additions can be removed. Laser marking is the opposite operation — it changes the surface itself, so the code is part of the board rather than something stuck onto it.

01

Labels fall off. Ink washes off.

The manufacturer's own comparison puts it plainly: the traditional label has low capacity, the mark falls off easily and is not durable, while the traditional inkjet code has low precision, a poor result, no permanence and high pollution with late investment. Both approaches also carry consumable and handling cost on every board. Laser marking needs no consumables.

02

Cleaning and soldering erode an added mark

A code on a PCB has to survive flux immersion, DI-water ultrasonic cleaning, silk-screen wash cycles and wave-soldering temperature. Those are exactly the conditions that attack an added film. Laser marking removes material instead of adding it, so there is nothing left for the process to strip away — the manufacturer reports no significant drop in code quality or readability after these operations.

03

Two sides means two decisions, not two machines

Boards that carry a code on both faces usually need either a second pass, a manual flip or a separate station — each with its own alignment error and its own labour. The S-400T reverses the board inside the machine and marks the second side at the same accuracy, so one in-line station delivers both faces.

02 — The marking cycle

Six steps, one pass, both faces

The cycle below is the sequence the S-400T runs on an SMEMA-connected line. Steps 1 to 4 mark side one; step 5 turns the board; step 6 repeats the cycle on side two and releases the board to the next machine. Conveyor width adjusts automatically, so a panel change does not need a mechanical reset.

STEP 1

Board transfer in

The panel enters on the conveyor under SMEMA handshake with the upstream machine. Conveyor height is 900 ± 20 mm and the rail width adjusts automatically to the board width, so the line keeps its pitch instead of waiting for a manual setup.

STEP 2

Clamp and locate

The board is fixed and the CCD plus Mark fiducial system finds its true position. Locating on fiducials rather than on the board edge is what makes the ±0.02 mm repeat accuracy meaningful on a panel that has already been through reflow and has expanded or shrunk.

STEP 3

Read the existing code

Where the panel already carries a bar code, the CCD reads it online before marking. That is what lets the wrong-material check work: an opposite, reversed or wrong board is detected before the laser fires, not after the panel has been scrapped.

STEP 4

Engrave and verify side one

The laser writes the code with the head moving over a stationary board. The same CCD then reads the fresh code back and grades its quality, so a marking failure is caught at the machine rather than at the customer's ICT station.

STEP 5

Invert the board

The built-in PCB reversal system turns the panel inside the machine and presents the second face at the same datum. This is the step that replaces a second machine, a manual flip or an offline marking bench — and it is why the S-400T is documented as a dual-side marking machine rather than a single-side marker with an accessory.

STEP 6

Mark, verify, release

Side two is marked and read back the same way, then the board releases downstream. With the optional bad-mark recognition function the machine reads the "X" positions on the panel and skips them, so a partly good panel is not lost to a marking error in a bad position.

MARK · LASER

The parts that decide whether the code is readable

CCD + Mark, not edge fixturing

Position is found from fiducial marks, not from the board edge. On a panel that has already survived reflow, the edge has moved and the fiducial has not — which is what makes ±0.02 mm repeat accuracy worth quoting.

Servo direct drive on X and Y

The marking head is driven directly by servo motors on both axes. Fewer mechanical stages between the motor and the head means less backlash to absorb, and less drift over a long production run.

Online grading, not a spot check

The same CCD that reads the incoming code reads the fresh one. Every board can be graded at the machine, so a drifting focus or a contaminated lens is caught on the panel it affects.

Smoke extraction built in

An automatic smoke purification system removes the dust and fume the marking process creates. That keeps the optical path clean — a dirty lens is the most common cause of a code that slowly stops reading — and keeps the fume out of the operator's breathing zone.

Wrong-board and bad-mark logic

Opposite, reversed and wrong-board recognition stops the laser firing on the wrong panel. The optional bad-mark function reads the panel's "X" positions and skips them, so a known-bad unit is not marked and does not enter the traceability record as a good one.

An interface your operators already know

The S-400T is documented with an operator interface available in English, and with an online bar code management system for building and editing the marking program. Board reversal inside the machine is what makes the second-side marking genuinely automatic rather than a manual step.

04 — Throughput

Throughput is a division, not a claim

A marking machine's output is the cycle time of one board divided into an hour. The manufacturer publishes a worked example: a 330 × 250 mm panel carrying one 2D code takes 3–4 s to load, 1 s for the fiducial mark, 0.5 s to engrave and 1 s to check — 5–7 s per board, about 600 boards per hour. Add codes, add a second side, and the number moves. The table below is that arithmetic, not a promise.

05 — Options and build decisions

Decide these six things before you order

The S-400T ships as a complete in-line marking station. These are the documented options and the standard equipment worth deciding on early, because a laser source chosen after the machine is built is a new head, not a setting.

Options as listed in the product document

Laser source and focal length

CO2, fiber, green or UV, with a focal length of 70, 110 or 190 mm. Focal length sets the working distance and the spot size, so it follows from the mark size you need and the height of the components around it.

Bar code grade analysis

An optional bar code level analysis system grades every printed code against a standard rather than simply confirming it was read. For automotive, medical and defence customers who must show a code met a grade, this is the difference between a reading and a record.

Bad-mark recognition

Automatically recognises the "X" positions on a panel and does not mark them. It stops a partly good panel being marked as though it were complete, and keeps the traceability record honest.

70 × 70 mm marking field

An optional enlarged marking field of 70 × 70 mm for panels that need a code, a logo and a date code placed away from each other, or a larger data-carrying symbol than the standard field allows.

Conveyor direction

Left to right is standard; right to left is an option. On a line where the marking station sits between two existing machines, direction is usually fixed by the layout and is worth confirming at the drawing stage rather than on site.

Factory system link

The S-400T is documented with access to SHOPFLOW, IMS and MES, plus customised intelligent management systems. The marking program and the traceability record can be driven by the shop-floor system rather than typed at the machine.

06 — Before the crate arrives

Six things the marking station expects from your floor

The S-400T is a light machine — 700 kg on a 1000 × 1600 mm footprint — and its services are modest compared with a reflow oven. That is exactly why the installation is usually simple, and exactly why the six items below are worth settling at the drawing stage: a missing air line stops the machine as effectively as a missing power feed.

STEP 1

Space and access

1000 × 1600 × 1700 mm footprint, 700 kg. Leave at least 800 mm clear at the front for loading the laser program and reaching the marking chamber, and keep the conveyor line clear on both sides so boards can be taken off for inspection. Avoid vibration sources and direct sunlight, which affect both the optics and the camera.

STEP 2

Power

AC 220 V, 16 A, 50/60 Hz. A single-phase feed is enough — there is no three-phase requirement in the specification and no water chiller to power. Feed the machine from the same distribution board as its line neighbours rather than from a shared socket circuit.

STEP 3

Compressed air

Clean, dry air at ≥ 0.5 MPa. The machine uses air for its smoke extraction and its pneumatic clamping. Damp air reaching the optics is the fastest way to spoil a marking result, so a dryer on the drop to the machine is worth the cost.

STEP 4

Fume extraction

Marking a solder mask produces fume — that is the nature of the process, not a fault. The S-400T carries its own automatic smoke purification system, but the extracted volume still has to go somewhere. Route it to the plant extraction duct, and think about it as a safety item rather than an accessory.

STEP 5

Line interface

SMEMA is the handshake. Confirm the conveyor height (900 ± 20 mm), the direction (left-to-right or right-to-left) and the interface type with the machines either side before the layout is frozen. If the marking station is not the only new machine on the line, agree the handshake in writing between suppliers.

STEP 6

Network and data

If the machine is to talk to MES, SHOPFLOW or IMS, the network drop and the addressing belong on the same checklist as the power feed. Agree who owns the interface — your IT team or the line integrator — before commissioning week rather than during it.

07 — Payback

Two ways to justify it — both with your numbers

A marking machine is bought against two costs. The first is the labour and consumables of the method it replaces — a label applicator, an inkjet head, or an operator who flips boards by hand. The second is the cost of a code that fails in the field. This calculator handles the first honestly. The second is the argument your quality manager already understands, and it is the larger of the two.

10 — Insights

Eight short reads on codes that have to stay readable

Everything we have learned putting marking machines onto EMS floors — written the way we explain it to customers: the problem first, a method you can reuse, and the honest numbers. Full articles are in English; summaries follow in your selected language.

ARTICLE 01The code that has to survive the wash line

A traceability code is only as good as the worst process it passes through. Here is how to find out which process that is — before you buy a marking machine.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document and the published laser specification table.

Walk to the end of your line and pick up a finished board. Look at the code. Now walk backwards and find every step that board passed through after the code was applied. That list — not the marking equipment — is what decides whether the code is still there in two years.

Most factories treat marking as a printing step and then subject the print to a chemical and thermal gauntlet. Flux immersion. DI-water ultrasonic cleaning. Stencil wash cycles. Wave-soldering temperature. Fingerprints from handling. Each of those is designed to remove material from a surface. If your code is a film sitting on that surface, the process is doing exactly what it was built to do.

Here is a method you can run this week without buying anything. Take ten boards. Mark them the way you mark today. Send five through your normal process and keep five as controls. Then read all ten under the same scanner, at the same distance, by the same person. Photograph every code. Lay the photographs side by side. What you are looking for is not a failure — it is a change. A code that reads but has lost contrast is a code that will stop reading in a year.

If the change is in the wash or the soldering step, that tells you the code has to be part of the surface rather than on top of it. This is the argument for laser marking: the process changes the solder mask itself, so there is no film for the wash to lift and no ink for the cleaner to dissolve. The S-400T engraves the code and then reads it back with the same CCD, so the verification record is generated at the machine rather than at the customer's incoming inspection.

Run the ten-board test again after the machine is installed, with the same five-and-five split. Repeat it every time you change solder mask supplier, board finish or cleaning chemistry. The code is a process output, and processes drift. A marking step you can re-verify in an afternoon is worth more than one you can only trust.

If you want to run the test on the S-400T instead of on your own bench, send us a panel with the code content you actually use and we will mark it and send back the images.

ARTICLE 02Why your 2D code stops reading at the ICT station

The code scans at the marking machine and fails three stations later. The cause is usually one of four things, and three of them are not the marking machine's fault.

Machine facts quoted here come from the S-400T product document.

A code that reads at the marking station and fails downstream is a specific, diagnosable event. It is not bad luck and it is rarely the laser. Before you call the marking supplier, separate the four possible causes.

One: the code moved. If the code is placed within a few millimetres of a board edge or a large component, handling equipment can shift the panel relative to the scanner's expected position. The fix is in the placement rule, not the marking machine.

Two: the contrast decayed. A mark that was dark when it was fresh can lighten after coating, cleaning or thermal cycling if it was made with the wrong wavelength for that solder mask. This is why the laser table matters. The manufacturer's own guidance says green and UV suit essentially all PCB solder-mask layers on the substrate, that green gives the highest precision and adhesion with UV close behind, that CO2 suits larger boards where the marking requirement is not high and can yellow or blacken, and that fiber is only partially suitable and needs a sample test first.

Three: the code failed a grade, not a read. A scanner in "read" mode returns yes or no. A scanner in grade mode returns a quality score. A code can pass the first and fail the second — and it is the grade that tells you whether the code will survive the next six months. This is what the S-400T's optional bar code level analysis system is for: it grades the fresh code at the machine, so a slowly degrading marking process is caught before it produces a shipment.

Four: the optical path is dirty. Marking a solder mask produces fume and dust. If the extraction is not doing its job, the lens gathers a film and the mark gets lighter over a shift. The S-400T carries an automatic smoke purification system for exactly this reason — and a daily lens check is still worth the thirty seconds.

So the method is: locate the failure, then ask which of the four it is. In our experience the answer is placement, wavelength or grade about four times out of five, and the marking machine about one time in five. Diagnose it in that order and you will spend your money in the right place.

ARTICLE 03Two sides, one station: what inline inversion changes

Marking both faces of a board usually costs you a second pass, a manual flip or a second machine. A built-in inverter collapses all three into one handling step.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

Ask a production engineer where boards get damaged and you will usually hear the same answer: between processes. Every time a panel is picked up, put down, flipped or re-staged, it accumulates handling damage, misalignment and labour. A marking step that requires a manual flip has added one of those events to every board you build.

The obvious alternative is two machines, one for each side. That works, and it costs twice the footprint, twice the power, twice the maintenance and a second alignment tolerance — the two sides are marked relative to two different datums, so a code on the top face and a code on the bottom face do not necessarily agree about where the board is.

A useful method when you are specifying any double-sided operation: count the handling events, then count the datums. Handling events are the opportunities for damage. Datums are the sources of error. A single station that marks both faces from one clamp wins on both counts, because the board is located once and turned inside the same fixture.

That is what the S-400T's built-in PCB reversal system does. The board is clamped, the fiducials are found, side one is marked and read, the inverter turns the panel inside the machine, and side two is marked and read against the same datum. The manufacturer documents the machine as a dual-side marking machine with the reversal system built in — not as a single-side marker with a handling accessory bolted on.

The second-order benefit is the one that shows up in the audit. Because both codes are read back by the same CCD in the same program, both sides of the traceability record are generated by the same station with the same grade analysis. When an auditor asks how you know the bottom code is good, the answer is not "an operator checked it". It is a stored read result from the machine that marked it.

If your product carries a code on both faces, tell us the board thickness, the component height on each side and the code position. Board thickness matters because the inverter has to handle 0.8 mm and 4 mm with the same reliability, and component clearance is documented as 18 mm above and 18 mm below the surface.

ARTICLE 04Choosing a wavelength for your solder mask

CO2, fiber, green or UV — the choice is not about power. It is about how the light couples into your specific solder mask, and that is testable.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

The most expensive mistake in laser marking is buying on wattage. Power tells you how fast the light can remove material. It tells you nothing about whether that material will absorb the light at all — and a solder mask that reflects your wavelength will mark badly no matter how many watts you point at it.

The S-400T accepts four sources, and the published table gives the wavelength of each: CO2 at 10.6 µm, fiber at 1064 nm, green at 535 nm and UV at 355 nm. Those are four very different interactions. The manufacturer's guidance is unusually direct about which to pick: green and UV are suitable for all PCB solder-mask layers on the substrate, green marks with high precision and strong adhesion, UV sits slightly behind green, CO2 suits larger boards where the requirement is not high and can yellow or blacken, and fiber is only partially suitable and requires a sample test.

Here is the method. Ask your solder mask supplier for the cure chemistry and the colour. Then ask for a marking sample on your own panel, in your own colour, from the machine supplier — not a demo panel in the colour that happens to be loaded. Mark the smallest code you actually intend to use, not a large one, because small marks are where wavelength differences show. Then send that sample through your real cleaning and soldering process and grade the code afterwards.

Two more variables belong in the decision. Focal length — 70, 110 or 190 mm on the S-400T — sets the working distance and the spot size, so a tall component beside the code decides which you can use. And the marking area you have to cover, documented as 1D 2 × 6 mm and 2D 1.5 × 1.5 mm per code, with an optional 70 × 70 mm field for panel-level work.

The acceptance evidence we can point to is a customer test on a UV source: 6 × 6 mm, 23-digit QR codes, marked directly from a program edited on site, at a 100 % success rate with no errors and no unclear codes — plus a reported minimum of 3 × 3 mm with 30 digits. That is a UV result, on that customer's board. It is evidence that UV works on that solder mask, not a claim about yours.

Send us three boards of the same product in the same colour and we will mark them with more than one source so you can compare the read results rather than the spec sheets.

ARTICLE 05How to calculate the marking station's real cycle time

Suppliers quote boards per hour. Your line only cares about seconds per board. Here is how to convert one into the other with your own numbers.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

A throughput figure is a division. It is one hour divided by the time one board takes. That means any throughput number you are quoted is really a statement about cycle time — and cycle time you can measure, add up and check.

The manufacturer of the S-400T publishes a worked example rather than a headline number, and it is worth copying the structure. A 330 × 250 mm panel carrying one 2D code: 3 to 4 seconds to load, 1 second for the fiducial mark, 0.5 seconds to engrave, 1 second to check. Total 5 to 7 seconds per board, about 600 boards per hour. Every one of those terms is a physical action you can watch and time.

So build your own version of that table, with four columns and one row per operation: load and transfer in, fiducial recognition, marking, read-back. Then multiply the marking and read-back rows by the number of codes per board — including the second side, if you are marking both. Add in the inverter step if the board is turned inside the machine. The sum is your cycle time.

Two honest corrections belong on the end. First, cycle time is not takt time. The marking station can be the fastest machine on the line and still be the constraint if it hands boards over in bursts; on a SMEMA line the station follows the pace of its neighbours. Second, the published numbers describe a machine in good condition. A contaminated lens and a worn extraction filter add seconds you will not find in the datasheet, which is why the daily lens check matters.

The S-400T also lets you trade cycle time against capability. Two codes instead of one roughly doubles the marking term. A larger marking field means more travel. A second side adds the inversion step and a second mark-and-read. That is not a weakness — it is the machine being honest about where the time goes, which makes it possible to design the marking step around your takt instead of hoping it fits.

Send us your operation list and your takt time and we will build the table with you. It takes one meeting and it removes the only number on the quotation that nobody can verify.

ARTICLE 06Sizing the machine to your takt, not to its headline speed

A marking machine that is faster than the line is not fast — it is a queue. Size the station to the pace of the process either side of it.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

There is a comfortable feeling in buying the fastest machine in a category. On a conveyor line it is usually the wrong instinct, and here is why: a marking station cannot run ahead of the boards arriving at it, and it cannot run behind the boards leaving it. Its useful speed is bounded by its neighbours.

So the first number to establish is not the machine's throughput. It is the takt of the process feeding it. If your wave-soldering line releases a panel every twenty seconds, a marking station that can do a panel in six seconds will spend fourteen seconds idle — every board, all shift. You have paid for capability that the line cannot use.

The method is to size against the constraint and leave the rest as headroom. Calculate the takt of the slowest machine on the line. Subtract your marking cycle time from it. If the result is comfortably positive, the marking station will never be the constraint and you should spend the remaining budget on capability instead of speed — a better laser source, the bar code grade analysis, or the bad-mark recognition that keeps the traceability record honest. If the result is negative, the board is too complex for one station and you need to look at splitting the marking load rather than buying a faster laser.

This is where the S-400T's configuration options become a sizing tool rather than a price list. The laser source determines the marking time. The focal length determines the working distance you can reach. The optional 70 × 70 mm marking field determines how much you can place in one pass. The second-side inverter determines whether you need one station or two. Choosing those four against your takt is a more useful exercise than comparing wattages.

One last sizing input that people forget: board thickness. The documented range is 0.8 to 4 mm, and both ends have to be handled reliably by the same conveyor and the same clamp. If your product mix spans that range, say so at specification stage, because that is a mechanical question and it is cheap to answer before the machine is built.

Bring us your line pitch and your board mix and we will size the station against the constraint rather than against the brochure.

ARTICLE 07From SHOPFLOW to MES: making marking a data source

A marking machine can be a printer on the line, or it can be the point where each board's identity enters your manufacturing system. The difference is an interface.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

Most factories can answer "how many boards did we build". Far fewer can answer "which board is this, what was it marked with, and did the mark read correctly". The second question is the one an auditor, a customer complaint or a field failure asks.

The gap is usually not the marking machine. It is that the marking step was never connected to anything. A code gets printed, an operator glances at it, and the only record is the board itself. If the code later turns out to be unreadable, there is no history to say when the process changed.

There is a straightforward method for closing that gap, and it works from either end. Start at the data: list the fields you actually want to hold against a board — the code content, the marking program version, the read result, the time, the operator or the line. Then work backwards to decide which of those the marking station must generate and which your MES already has. Only then look at interfaces. Factories that start with the interface usually end up logging the one field the machine happens to output.

The S-400T is documented with system access to SHOPFLOW, IMS and MES, plus customised intelligent management systems. It reads an existing code online before marking and reads the fresh code afterwards, and it supports the wrong-material checks — opposite, reversed and wrong board — that only make sense when the machine knows what it is supposed to be marking. The optional bad-mark recognition reads the "X" positions on a panel and skips them, which keeps the record free of boards that were never good.

One practical instruction: agree who owns the interface before commissioning week. If the machine is to talk to your MES, someone has to own the data mapping, and it is usually not the equipment supplier. Put that on the same checklist as the power feed and the network drop, and the marking step arrives as a data source rather than as a printer.

ARTICLE 08The consumable you stop buying when you mark with light

Labels, ink, ribbon and the operator time to apply them are a cost that repeats on every board you build. Laser marking replaces that with a capital cost and an electricity bill.

Articles are marketing commentary. Machine facts quoted inside them come from the S-400T product document.

Consumable costs are easy to underestimate because they are small and they never stop. A label is a few cents. Ink is a fraction of a cent per board. Someone applies them, someone replaces the roll, someone reprints the ones that go on crooked. Individually trivial; multiplied by every board you build for ten years, not trivial at all.

The manufacturer's own comparison between the marking methods is blunt about the trade. The traditional label has low capacity, the mark falls off easily and is not durable, and the total investment is high. The traditional inkjet code has low precision, a poor result, no permanence, high pollution and late investment. Against both, laser marking is described as clear and long-lasting, high efficiency, environmentally friendly and free of consumables — low input, high return.

Here is how to put a number on it. Multiply your consumable cost per board — label, ink, ribbon, reprints — by your monthly volume, and by twelve. Add the labour of application at a loaded hourly rate. Now compare that annual figure with the price of a marking station. That ratio is the part of the payback you can compute without assuming anything about quality. The calculator on this page does exactly that arithmetic with your numbers.

The second half of the return is the one that is harder to compute and usually larger. Every label that falls off in the field is a traceability gap, a possible recall of a wider batch than necessary, and sometimes a warranty claim on a board that was actually built correctly. Removing the adhesive film removes the failure mode. Laser marking changes the solder mask itself, so there is nothing to peel, nothing to wash off and nothing to reprint.

The honest counter-argument is capital. A marking station is a purchase, and the consumables were an operating cost. That is a real change in how the money leaves the business, and it needs to be a deliberate decision rather than a happy accident. Run the arithmetic on your own volumes, then decide whether you want the cost to be variable or fixed.

The calculator above will do it with your figures. If you send us your volume and your consumable cost per board, we will send back the ratio with the assumptions written out so your finance team can check them.

13 — FAQ

The questions this machine raises in a first meeting

What exactly does the S-400T do?
It is an automatic in-line laser marking machine for PCBs that marks both faces of a board in one pass. A panel enters on the conveyor from an SMEMA handshake, CCD plus fiducial Mark recognition finds its true position, the laser engraves the code, and the CCD reads it back and checks the quality. A built-in PCB reversal system then turns the board inside the machine and the cycle repeats on the second side. The laser head can be built around a CO2, fiber, green or UV source.
What board sizes and thicknesses can it handle?
The published specification lists a PCB range of minimum 50 × 80 mm to maximum 450 × 400 mm, with board thickness 0.8–4 mm and component clearance of 18 mm above and 18 mm below the board surface. Conveyor width adjusts automatically and conveyor height is 900 ± 20 mm. If your board sits outside that envelope, the S-4545DT in the same family is the larger platform to look at.
Which laser source should I choose?
The S-400T accepts CO2 at 10.6 µm, fiber at 1064 nm, green at 535 nm and UV at 355 nm, at the power levels in the laser table. The manufacturer's guidance: green and UV suit all PCB solder-mask layers on the substrate, with green giving the highest precision and adhesion and UV slightly behind; CO2 suits larger boards where the marking requirement is not high but can yellow or blacken; fiber is only partially suitable and needs a sample test. The only reliable selection method is a marking sample on your own board, in your own colour, sent through your own process.
How fast is it, really?
Throughput is one hour divided by the cycle time of a board, and the manufacturer publishes a worked example rather than a headline figure: for a 330 × 250 mm panel with one 2D code, 3–4 s to load, 1 s for the fiducial, 0.5 s to engrave and 1 s to check — 5–7 s per board, about 600 boards per hour. A verified customer test on a UV source recorded up to 700 boards per hour marking 6 × 6 mm, 23-digit QR codes. Your number will differ with the code count, the second side and the marking area, so we calculate it from your board rather than quoting the table.
Does the mark survive wave soldering, washing and ultrasonic cleaning?
Laser marking changes the solder mask itself instead of adding a film on top of it, so there is no adhesive to lift and no ink to dissolve. The manufacturer reports that they tested against real production conditions — stencil-printing wash cycles, fingerprint contamination and high-temperature furnace exposure — and found no significant effect on code quality or readability. We would still verify it on your own board finish: send us a panel and we will mark it and put it through your process before you commit.
Can it connect to our MES, and what about bad panels?
The S-400T is documented with system access to SHOPFLOW, IMS, MES and customised intelligent management systems, and it reads an existing code online before marking as well as reading the fresh code afterwards. Wrong-material recognition covers opposite, reversed and wrong-board conditions, so the laser does not fire on the wrong panel. The optional bad-mark recognition function reads the "X" positions on a panel and does not mark them, and the optional bar code level analysis system grades every code rather than simply confirming that it was read.
